detailed_rationale:
HAL closed FY26 (year to Mar-2026) with standalone revenue from operations of Rs 33,090 cr (+~7% YoY) and standalone PAT of Rs 9,076 cr (+9.1% YoY; consolidated PAT Rs 9,116 cr). Full-year EBITDA margin held at ~30% (Rs 13,472 cr, +11% YoY), though Q4 FY26 alone showed margin compression of ~235-237bps YoY to 36.3%, management attributing this to one-off employee-cost charges of roughly Rs 491 cr rather than a structural cost problem. Materially, Rs 3,704 cr of FY26 profit (vs Rs 2,566 cr in FY25) came from other/treasury income earned on HAL's Rs 42,425 cr cash-and-deposit pile (up from Rs 33,624 cr) -- back-of-envelope against an estimated ~Rs 12,000-12,300 cr PBT (grossing up PAT at HAL's ~25% effective tax rate), that is roughly 30% of pre-tax profit coming from interest income, not operations. This is a real profit-quality flag: a chunk of the 9%+ profit growth was rate-cycle-driven, and would fade if RBI easing compresses deposit yields over the next 1-2 years, absent commensurate rate cuts on HAL's own cost of funds (which is not a meaningful offset since HAL carries negligible debt).

The order book stands at a record Rs 2,54,538 cr (up from Rs 1,89,302 cr a year earlier), against FY26 revenue of ~Rs 33,090 cr -- roughly 7-8 years of revenue cover, and this is real, MoD-contracted backlog (not MOUs/LoIs), with ~95% of orders originating from a single customer, the Indian Armed Forces. Fresh FY26 order inflow was Rs 97,028 cr (Rs 69,668 cr manufacturing + Rs 26,539 cr ROH), including 97 LCA Mk1A, 6 ALH Mk III MR and 8 Do-228 aircraft. Repair/overhaul (ROH) contributes an estimated 40-45% of recurring revenue and is the stable, margin-predictable half of the business (~8% CAGR expected through FY28E); manufacturing is the high-growth, high-execution-risk half. On execution: HAL has built, flown and ground-tested ~30 Tejas Mk1A airframes but formal IAF handover has been stalled for over a year awaiting GE F404-IN20 engines -- only 6 engines delivered and under airframe integration as of mid-2026, against a GE commitment of 20 more in H2 2026 (a prior March-2026 sub-deadline for 5 engines was already missed), 24 in FY27, and 30/year from FY28-29. HAL/IAF guidance now points to first Mk1A deliveries in Aug-Sep 2026 with ~20-24 aircraft in FY27 -- the third or fourth slippage of this delivery timeline since the original 2021 contract (83 aircraft; a further 97-aircraft, ~$7bn firm order was signed in Sept-2025, a completed contract, taking total Mk1A firm orders to ~180). Tejas Mk2 has also slipped: earlier guidance pointed to a Q1-2026 first flight, the latest (Jul-2026) management commentary points to prototype rollout only by Mar-2027. Separately, HAL was excluded from India's 5th-generation AMCA fighter program in 2026 -- that development track now sits with a Tata / L&T(-BEL-Dynamatic) / Bharat Forge(-BEML-Data Patterns) shortlist -- removing HAL's clearest next-decade growth optionality beyond the current Tejas/helicopter/engine-JV backlog. Management's own FY27 guidance is a comparatively modest 10-12% revenue growth with margins normalized at 30-31%, i.e. management itself is not underwriting a re-acceleration story.

Q1 FY27 (Jun-2026 quarter) results were not yet out as of this review (2026-07-19); no confirmed reporting date was found in the search, but HAL (like most PSUs) typically reports Q1 in mid-to-late August (last year's Q1 FY26 print was 12-Aug-2025), so the print is imminent within weeks. The stock trades at ~32-33x trailing earnings (5-year average ~28.7x), ROE ~24%, ROCE ~32%, against management's own 10-12% guided growth -- a PEG of roughly 2.7-3x on the guided number. That multiple is being paid for a near-monopoly, government-backed order book with genuine multi-year revenue visibility, but it is also being paid on top of (i) a single foreign-supplier engine bottleneck with a two-year-plus track record of missed delivery deadlines on the company's single largest volume driver, (ii) ~30% of reported profit coming from a treasury-income tailwind that is not permanent, and (iii) the recent loss of the AMCA growth option. None of these are fatal to the business -- HAL is not going away, and the ROH annuity plus existing Tejas/helicopter backlog gives a very long execution runway -- but the price already assumes smooth, on-schedule delivery of a program that has not once, in its history, delivered on schedule.
recommendation_rationale: This is a valuation-and-execution-quality call, not a business-quality call. HAL's underlying franchise (near-monopoly IAF supplier, 7-8 years of contracted revenue visibility, 24% ROE, 30%+ ROCE, stable ROH annuity) would comfortably support a Hold or even better at a reasonable multiple. But at ~32-33x trailing earnings -- above its own 5-year average -- against management's own 10-12% FY27 growth guidance, with (a) a recurring, multi-year engine-supply bottleneck on the single biggest near-term delivery driver that has missed deadlines repeatedly and as recently as Mar-2026, (b) ~30% of FY26 profit attributable to treasury/interest income that is exposed to a rate-cut cycle, and (c) the recent exclusion from the AMCA 5th-gen fighter program removing the clearest next-decade growth funnel, the multiple is pricing smoother execution and more growth durability than the evidence supports. The call is Sell on richness-versus-delivered-growth mismatch, not on any doubt about HAL's franchise durability.
summary: Hindustan Aeronautics is India's dominant military aircraft maker with a record Rs 2.54 lakh crore order book -- about 7-8 years of current revenue -- almost entirely from the Indian Armed Forces, and strong returns (ROE ~24%, ROCE ~32%). But the stock's ~32-33x earnings multiple is being paid for smooth execution of the Tejas Mk1A fighter program that has repeatedly slipped for over two years because of delayed engine supply from its US partner GE, with only 6 of the needed engines delivered so far and first jet deliveries now guided to Aug-Sep 2026. About 30% of last year's profit came from interest earned on HAL's large cash pile rather than from the core aircraft business, and HAL was recently dropped from India's next-generation fighter (AMCA) program, narrowing its future growth options. Management's own guidance for next year is a modest 10-12% revenue growth. Given the price already assumes a smoother delivery record than HAL has actually shown, we rate this a Sell on valuation versus realistically achievable growth, while flagging that the underlying government-backed franchise itself remains sound.
positive_para: HAL sits at the center of India's defence-indigenization push with a near-monopoly position supplying fighters, trainers and helicopters to the Indian Armed Forces, and its order book has grown to a record Rs 2.54 lakh crore (from Rs 1.89 lakh crore a year earlier) -- roughly 7-8 years of revenue already contracted, not merely announced. These are firm MoD orders, not intentions: a fresh, signed Rs ~58,000-crore-plus (97-aircraft, ~$7bn) Tejas Mk1A contract was concluded in Sept-2025 on top of the original 2021 order, taking firm Mk1A orders to ~180 aircraft. The Repair/Overhaul (ROH) business, an estimated 40-45% of recurring revenue, is a stable, high-visibility annuity largely insulated from manufacturing-ramp risk. Returns are excellent (ROE ~24%, ROCE ~32%, EBITDA margin ~30%), the balance sheet is debt-light with a Rs 42,425 crore cash/deposit pile, the company pays a large dividend (Rs 35/share, 700% of face value for FY26), and the first Tejas Mk1A engines have finally started arriving (6 delivered, integration underway) with formal deliveries now guided for Aug-Sep 2026 -- suggesting the multi-year engine bottleneck, while not resolved, is at least easing. Persistent India-Pakistan border tension (ceasefire from May-2025 still holds but rhetoric continues into mid-2026) keeps the broader defence-order-flow and budget tailwind intact.
negative_para: The bear case is that the market is paying a premium multiple (~32-33x, above HAL's own 5-year average of ~28.7x) for a growth story that management itself only guides at 10-12% for FY27, and that this modest guide already reflects genuine, repeated execution risk rather than conservatism. The Tejas Mk1A program -- HAL's single largest near-term delivery driver -- has slipped its formal IAF handover for more than two years because of GE F404 engine delays; only 6 of the needed engines have arrived, GE has already missed one interim 2026 deadline (5 engines due Mar-2026), and the promised ramp to 20 engines in H2-2026 and 30/year from FY28-29 rests on a supplier with a poor recent track record on this exact program. Roughly 30% of FY26 pre-tax profit came from interest earned on HAL's cash pile rather than core operations -- a tailwind that fades as/if rates ease, meaning reported profit growth has been flattered by a non-operational item. HAL was also excluded from India's 5th-generation AMCA fighter development program in 2026 (awarded instead to a Tata/L&T-BEL-Dynamatic/Bharat Forge-BEML-Data Patterns shortlist), removing its clearest visible growth option beyond the existing Tejas/helicopter/ROH backlog, and the follow-on Tejas Mk2 program has itself slipped roughly a year on prototype timelines. At today's price, very little room exists for another delivery delay or for the treasury-income tailwind to unwind without a genuine earnings disappointment.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~32-33x trailing earnings (versus a 5-year average of ~28.7x) and management's own 10-12% FY27 revenue-growth guidance, the multiple implies a PEG of roughly 2.7-3x on guided growth -- i.e., the market is pricing durable double-digit-plus growth with clean, on-schedule execution of the Tejas Mk1A ramp and continued margin stability, essentially assuming the current engine-supply bottleneck resolves smoothly and stays resolved. HAL's actual delivery history on this exact program says otherwise: the Mk1A handover has slipped three-to-four times over more than two years on a single foreign supplier's engine deliveries, and a sub-deadline was missed as recently as Mar-2026. Layer on that ~30% of FY26 pre-tax profit came from treasury income (not core operations) that is vulnerable to a rate-easing cycle, and the loss of AMCA as a next-decade growth option, and the multiple looks priced for a smoother, more linear delivery curve than HAL's execution record supports. The order-book depth (7-8 years of revenue) and ROH annuity justify a premium to the market, but not the current premium to HAL's own history -- this reads rich rather than cheap or fair.
